The **Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency** (**DARPA**) is a research and development agency of the United States Department of Defense responsible for the development of emerging technologies for use by the military.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-4) Originally known as the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA), the agency was created on February 7, 1958, by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in response to the Soviets' launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957. By collaborating with academia, industry, and government partners, DARPA formulates and executes research and development projects to expand the frontiers of technology and science, often beyond immediate U.S. military requirements.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-Commission2008-5) The name of the organization was first changed from its founding name, ARPA, to DARPA, in March 1972, changing back to ARPA in February 1993, then reverted back to DARPA in March 1996.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-6)
_The Economist_ has called DARPA "the agency that shaped the modern world", with technologies such as "Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine ... weather satellites, GPS, drones, stealth technology, voice interfaces, the personal computer, and the internet on the list of innovations for which DARPA can claim at least partial credit".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-Economist-7) Its track record of success has inspired governments around the world to launch similar research and development agencies.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-Economist-7)

DARPA is independent of other military research and development and reports directly to senior Department of Defense management. # What was ARPANET? When was it invented?
The creation of the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) was authorized by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in 1958 (official start date: February 7, 1958) for the purpose of forming and executing research and development projects to expand the frontiers of technology and science, and able to reach far beyond immediate military requirements, the two relevant acts being the Supplemental Military Construction Authorization (Air Force) and Department of Defense Directive, in February 1958. Its creation was directly attributed to the launching of Sputnik and to U.S. realization that the Soviet Union had developed the capacity to rapidly exploit military technology. Initial funding of ARPA was $520 million. ARPA's first director, Roy Johnson, left a $160,000 management job at General Electric for an $18,000 job at ARPA. Herbert York from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory was hired as his scientific assistant. One of the first assignments tasked to ARPA was research into an "undownable" computer system. At that time, all large companies, and most countries (including the United States) were dependent on a single Main Frame computer to store electronic data, and it was accessed by, what was referred to as, “Dumb Terminals”. These “Dumb Terminal” stations had no real computer power, other than the ability to access the Main Frame. This is not to say that the entire United States government had all of its data on a single Main Frame, but each agency had a Main Frame where their particular data was stored and accessed. This made the computer system and information very vulnerable to being shut down. A single well-placed bomb (even a small bomb) could not only prevent everyone and anyone from accessing the data, but totally destroying the data. One of the first tasks of ARPA was to find a way to prevent that possibility. That, of course, was the beginning of the Internet we have today. Initially, the name of this new “undownable” network was “ARPANet”.

ARPANET was an early computer networking technology that was developed in the late 1960s. It served as the precursor to modern-day internet technologies and allowed for large-scale computer networking between different institutions and research centers. ARPANET was officially decommissioned in 1990.
ARPANET was developed by a team of researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in the late 1960s. The project was funded by the United States Department of Defense, and its primary purpose was to allow for large-scale computer networking between different research institutions and defense agencies. The first ARPANET network went online in 1969 and consisted of four nodes: two at MIT, one at Stanford University, and one at the University of California, Los Angeles.
The early days of ARPANET were marked by instability and frequent outages. However, the technology continued to develop and evolve over the years. In 1981, the ARPANET network was divided into two separate networks: the ARPANET network and the MILNET network. The ARPANET network was used for research and education purposes, while the MILNET network was used for military communications.
ARPANET was officially decommissioned in 1990. By that time, newer and more advanced networking technologies had emerged, such as TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol), which is still used today. Nevertheless, ARPANET played a significant role.

## Full article
The _Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA)_ is part of the US Department of Defense. This agency produces and tests technology and equipment for the government and the military. DARPA's main mission is to create advanced technology for national security. In 2024, approximately 70% of DARPA programs use some form of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, or autonomous technology, highlighting the agency's strong focus on developing intelligent systems. The agency researches hundreds of projects, many of which are highly classified, at any given time. DARPA has helped create many important technologies, including the Internet. The agency has also seen many large, expensive failures; nevertheless, these failures have helped lead to important technological advances.

## Full article
### Background
After World War II ended in the 1940s, the United States and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) became the leading superpowers in the world. These two countries eventually became embroiled in the Cold War (1947–91), during which both tried to have the most advanced technology. In 1957, the USSR government changed history by successfully launching Sputnik I, the first artificial satellite successfully launched into space. The United States government realized that this technological advancement had far-reaching implications for communication, intelligence, and defense. The launch of Sputnik also began the space race between the United States and the USSR. US president Dwight Eisenhower realized that the United States had to work to gain the same and even more advanced technology than the USSR. In 1958, DARPA, which was first called the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA), was launched. The original role of the agency was to be the military space program in the United States. That same year, the agency that would become the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) was also formed, and it was to serve as the nation's civilian space exploration program. At first, all the satellite projects being undertaken by the US government were being run through DARPA. At the time the agency was established, it was also hoped that it would help develop advanced weapons systems.
Within a few years of its formation, DARPA had all its satellite and space programs taken away. The army, navy, and air force took over their own satellite programs, and NASA took over all the civilian space programs. This left DARPA without a mission. Yet, instead of fading away, DARPA reinvented itself. William Godel, a scientist at DARPA, realized that the agency needed a new mission, and he believed the agency should begin to focus on strategic threats. He and others inside the agency tried to determine which threats would be most important to the United States in the coming years. Godel believed that the biggest threat the United States would face in the future was insurgent forces because he thought the United States would fight wars against small communist countries.

## Full article
### Background
Godel and others inside DARPA were correct in their assumptions about the threats the United States would face. In the 1960s and 1970s, the United States fought a difficult war in Vietnam against an insurgent force. The United States infamously used one of DARPA's inventions, Agent Orange, during that conflict. Agent Orange was a defoliant, or a chemical that kills the leaves on trees and other plants. DARPA created chemical defoliants so the military could remove the leaves from plants to better identify insurgent forces in jungle areas, such as Vietnam. During the Vietnam War, the United States used Agent Orange to locate insurgent forces in thick jungles. Nevertheless, it also used the chemical on the enemy's crops. Years later, Vietnamese citizens and American soldiers experienced serious health disorders because of exposure to the chemical.
After the Vietnam War, DARPA came under scrutiny for its role in the war. The American public and politicians had begun to lose faith in the organization. During the latter part of the Cold War, DARPA focused its efforts on developing advanced weapons systems. DARPA's mission changed again only a few decades later after the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. After these attacks, the agency began to focus on data collection and using data to try to predict terrorist activity. Eventually, people became concerned that DARPA's work with personal data could lead to invasions of privacy. Therefore, the data collection and analysis projects were shut down.

## Full article
### Topic Today
DARPA is best known to the public for its help in developing some of the most important technologies people use in the modern world. The most famous example of a vital modern technology that DARPA helped create is the Internet. ARPANET, which was the technology created by DARPA, was a network created so that computers could communicate with one another. This technology eventually led to the Internet, which billions of people use every day. DARPA also played an important role in helping to develop global positioning systems (GPS), which help people find their destinations using digital maps and other digital GPS devices. While DARPA has helped develop many vital technologies, it has also experienced many failures. For example, the National Aero-Space Plane was a proposed technology that was supposed to send a plane from a runway into the atmosphere and eventually into space without the use of rockets. Although the technology seemed useful, DARPA was unable to produce a working model. However, even some of DARPA's technological failures have been important, as they have provided vital information for other researchers.
DARPA’s FY2026 enacted budget was $4.322 billion, funding classified and public research in areas such as AI, advanced military technology, cybersecurity, and biotechnology. DARPA works on hundreds of projects at a time. The agency works on so many projects at once because its leaders understand that only some of these projects will be successful.
In the twenty-first century, the agency was working on a number of technologies that could go on to help shape national defense in the United States for years to come. For example, Extreme Accuracy Tasked Ordnance (EXACTO) is a bullet that changes trajectory during flight. These bullets will change their trajectory to account for the movement of a target and for other factors (such as wind). DARPA was also working on a system similar to GPS that used Earth's magnetic field rather than satellites to give exact locations. By 2024, DARPA was investigating the possibility of using weapon systems operated by artificial intelligence (AI). The group hoped to discover if AI weapon systems could make ethical decisions. In 2026, DARPA and the US Air Force successfully tested an AI-controlled F-16 through the VENOM program, advancing autonomous flight technology. The program aims to improve human-machine teaming by allowing AI systems to assist pilots in future air combat operations.

## Full article
### Background
After World War II ended in the 1940s, the United States and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) became the leading superpowers in the world. These two countries eventually became embroiled in the Cold War (1947–91), during which both tried to have the most advanced technology. In 1957, the USSR government changed history by successfully launching Sputnik I, the first artificial satellite successfully launched into space. The United States government realized that this technological advancement had far-reaching implications for communication, intelligence, and defense. The launch of Sputnik also began the space race between the United States and the USSR. US president Dwight Eisenhower realized that the United States had to work to gain the same and even more advanced technology than the USSR. In 1958, DARPA, which was first called the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA), was launched. The original role of the agency was to be the military space program in the United States. That same year, the agency that would become the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) was also formed, and it was to serve as the nation's civilian space exploration program. At first, all the satellite projects being undertaken by the US government were being run through DARPA. At the time the agency was established, it was also hoped that it would help develop advanced weapons systems.
Within a few years of its formation, DARPA had all its satellite and space programs taken away. The army, navy, and air force took over their own satellite programs, and NASA took over all the civilian space programs. This left DARPA without a mission. Yet, instead of fading away, DARPA reinvented itself. William Godel, a scientist at DARPA, realized that the agency needed a new mission, and he believed the agency should begin to focus on strategic threats. He and others inside the agency tried to determine which threats would be most important to the United States in the coming years. Godel believed that the biggest threat the United States would face in the future was insurgent forces because he thought the United States would fight wars against small communist countries.

## Full article
### Background
Godel and others inside DARPA were correct in their assumptions about the threats the United States would face. In the 1960s and 1970s, the United States fought a difficult war in Vietnam against an insurgent force. The United States infamously used one of DARPA's inventions, Agent Orange, during that conflict. Agent Orange was a defoliant, or a chemical that kills the leaves on trees and other plants. DARPA created chemical defoliants so the military could remove the leaves from plants to better identify insurgent forces in jungle areas, such as Vietnam. During the Vietnam War, the United States used Agent Orange to locate insurgent forces in thick jungles. Nevertheless, it also used the chemical on the enemy's crops. Years later, Vietnamese citizens and American soldiers experienced serious health disorders because of exposure to the chemical.
After the Vietnam War, DARPA came under scrutiny for its role in the war. The American public and politicians had begun to lose faith in the organization. During the latter part of the Cold War, DARPA focused its efforts on developing advanced weapons systems. DARPA's mission changed again only a few decades later after the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. After these attacks, the agency began to focus on data collection and using data to try to predict terrorist activity. Eventually, people became concerned that DARPA's work with personal data could lead to invasions of privacy. Therefore, the data collection and analysis projects were shut down.

## Full article
### Topic Today
DARPA is best known to the public for its help in developing some of the most important technologies people use in the modern world. The most famous example of a vital modern technology that DARPA helped create is the Internet. ARPANET, which was the technology created by DARPA, was a network created so that computers could communicate with one another. This technology eventually led to the Internet, which billions of people use every day. DARPA also played an important role in helping to develop global positioning systems (GPS), which help people find their destinations using digital maps and other digital GPS devices. While DARPA has helped develop many vital technologies, it has also experienced many failures. For example, the National Aero-Space Plane was a proposed technology that was supposed to send a plane from a runway into the atmosphere and eventually into space without the use of rockets. Although the technology seemed useful, DARPA was unable to produce a working model. However, even some of DARPA's technological failures have been important, as they have provided vital information for other researchers.
DARPA’s FY2026 enacted budget was $4.322 billion, funding classified and public research in areas such as AI, advanced military technology, cybersecurity, and biotechnology. DARPA works on hundreds of projects at a time. The agency works on so many projects at once because its leaders understand that only some of these projects will be successful.
In the twenty-first century, the agency was working on a number of technologies that could go on to help shape national defense in the United States for years to come. For example, Extreme Accuracy Tasked Ordnance (EXACTO) is a bullet that changes trajectory during flight. These bullets will change their trajectory to account for the movement of a target and for other factors (such as wind). DARPA was also working on a system similar to GPS that used Earth's magnetic field rather than satellites to give exact locations. By 2024, DARPA was investigating the possibility of using weapon systems operated by artificial intelligence (AI). The group hoped to discover if AI weapon systems could make ethical decisions. In 2026, DARPA and the US Air Force successfully tested an AI-controlled F-16 through the VENOM program, advancing autonomous flight technology. The program aims to improve human-machine teaming by allowing AI systems to assist pilots in future air combat operations.

# What was ARPANET? When was it invented?
The creation of the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) was authorized by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in 1958 (official start date: February 7, 1958) for the purpose of forming and executing research and development projects to expand the frontiers of technology and science, and able to reach far beyond immediate military requirements, the two relevant acts being the Supplemental Military Construction Authorization (Air Force) and Department of Defense Directive, in February 1958. Its creation was directly attributed to the launching of Sputnik and to U.S. realization that the Soviet Union had developed the capacity to rapidly exploit military technology. Initial funding of ARPA was $520 million. ARPA's first director, Roy Johnson, left a $160,000 management job at General Electric for an $18,000 job at ARPA. Herbert York from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory was hired as his scientific assistant. One of the first assignments tasked to ARPA was research into an "undownable" computer system. At that time, all large companies, and most countries (including the United States) were dependent on a single Main Frame computer to store electronic data, and it was accessed by, what was referred to as, “Dumb Terminals”. These “Dumb Terminal” stations had no real computer power, other than the ability to access the Main Frame. This is not to say that the entire United States government had all of its data on a single Main Frame, but each agency had a Main Frame where their particular data was stored and accessed. This made the computer system and information very vulnerable to being shut down. A single well-placed bomb (even a small bomb) could not only prevent everyone and anyone from accessing the data, but totally destroying the data. One of the first tasks of ARPA was to find a way to prevent that possibility. That, of course, was the beginning of the Internet we have today. Initially, the name of this new “undownable” network was “ARPANet”.

ARPANET was an early computer networking technology that was developed in the late 1960s. It served as the precursor to modern-day internet technologies and allowed for large-scale computer networking between different institutions and research centers. ARPANET was officially decommissioned in 1990.
ARPANET was developed by a team of researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in the late 1960s. The project was funded by the United States Department of Defense, and its primary purpose was to allow for large-scale computer networking between different research institutions and defense agencies. The first ARPANET network went online in 1969 and consisted of four nodes: two at MIT, one at Stanford University, and one at the University of California, Los Angeles.
The early days of ARPANET were marked by instability and frequent outages. However, the technology continued to develop and evolve over the years. In 1981, the ARPANET network was divided into two separate networks: the ARPANET network and the MILNET network. The ARPANET network was used for research and education purposes, while the MILNET network was used for military communications.
ARPANET was officially decommissioned in 1990. By that time, newer and more advanced networking technologies had emerged, such as TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol), which is still used today. Nevertheless, ARPANET played a significant role.

The **Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency** (**DARPA**) is a research and development agency of the United States Department of Defense responsible for the development of emerging technologies for use by the military.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-4) Originally known as the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA), the agency was created on February 7, 1958, by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in response to the Soviets' launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957. By collaborating with academia, industry, and government partners, DARPA formulates and executes research and development projects to expand the frontiers of technology and science, often beyond immediate U.S. military requirements.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-Commission2008-5) The name of the organization was first changed from its founding name, ARPA, to DARPA, in March 1972, changing back to ARPA in February 1993, then reverted back to DARPA in March 1996.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-6)
_The Economist_ has called DARPA "the agency that shaped the modern world", with technologies such as "Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine ... weather satellites, GPS, drones, stealth technology, voice interfaces, the personal computer, and the internet on the list of innovations for which DARPA can claim at least partial credit".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-Economist-7) Its track record of success has inspired governments around the world to launch similar research and development agencies.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA#cite_note-Economist-7)

The creation of the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) was authorized by President Dwight D. Its creation was directly attributed to the launching of Sputnik and to U.S. realization that the Soviet Union had developed the capacity to rapidly exploit military technology. Initial funding of ARPA was $520 million. ARPA's first director, Roy Johnson, left a $160,000 management job at General Electric for an $18,000 job at ARPA. Herbert York from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory was hired as his scientific assistant. One of the first assignments tasked to ARPA was research into an "undownable" computer system. At that time, all large companies, and most countries (including the United States) were dependent on a single Main Frame computer to store electronic data, and it was accessed by, what was referred to as, “Dumb Terminals”. These “Dumb Terminal” stations had no real computer power, other than the ability to access the Main Frame. This is not to say that the entire United States government had all of its data on a single Main Frame, but each agency had a Main Frame where their particular data was stored and accessed. This made the computer system and information very vulnerable to being shut down. A single well-placed bomb (even a small bomb) could not only prevent everyone and anyone from accessing the data, but totally destroying the data. One of the first tasks of ARPA was to find a way to prevent that possibility. That, of course, was the beginning of the Internet we have today. Initially, the name of this new “undownable” network was “ARPANet”.

ARPANET was developed by a team of researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in the late 1960s. The project was funded by the United States Department of Defense, and its primary purpose was to allow for large-scale computer networking between different research institutions and defense agencies. The first ARPANET network went online in 1969 and consisted of four nodes: two at MIT, one at Stanford University, and one at the University of California, Los Angeles.
The early days of ARPANET were marked by instability and frequent outages. However, the technology continued to develop and evolve over the years. In 1981, the ARPANET network was divided into two separate networks: the ARPANET network and the MILNET network. The ARPANET network was used for research and education purposes, while the MILNET network was used for military communications.
ARPANET was officially decommissioned in 1990. By that time, newer and more advanced networking technologies had emerged, such as TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol), which is still used today. Nevertheless, ARPANET played a significant role.
